For the purposes of this forecast, a "correct" solution that changes the definition of P is acceptable. On the other hand, a differential equation and Turing-computation definitions of NP are unsatisfying; a solution may give preferred unique solutions for instances of NP that map reasonably to physical processes but this solution contain an algorithm that is only observable indirectly. On the other hand, it would seem that for the purpose of a Clay Mathematics Institute prize, all that is required is producing a published solution meeting the mathematical definition as defined on the website.

The constraint that the sentence above be simplified in a realistic and convincing way requires combining reasoning steps, and its indirect language - "that can't quickly be corrected" and "many years to refute the proof" - are nonliteral; 20 years, with a standard alpha, are unlikely for a value of 1-0.99-.01. 

I do expect hard-E as long as hard-NP remains, and I do expect this to happen long before a proof of the weak implication that P is the least over all E for which P = E. 

Additional notes beyond the forecast
At the time of the forecast: 

* The presumption is that the problem will likely remain open in consideration of the new definition. Taking the definition to include a conjecture over NP and Turing-computable problems, this would allow pointer-chasing O(log(n)) programs using bounded memory, NP-complete problems that are in fact listable and NP-complete simulated on a Turing machine, and so forth. 

* By condition 2 description of a large unsatisfiable Boolean formula that encodes SAT, a solution would lower the bound or prove that P is not NP. However, this condition does not preclude a lower bound, by proving that SAT forms a basis for NP. A satisfying proof that P is not NP but does not prove NP-complete cannot exist, given that P = NP and P not NP each imply the other.

* Due to low complexity for classes like P^NP and P^BPP, condition 3 should be dropped and not trivialized.

* Condition 4 adequately mirrors what is presented on the site, without requiring a typical NP-complete problem composition, balancing the specifics of a fixed possible input against the listable nature of more interestingly P-hard problems. Condition 1, referencing functions, can be unnecessary given that a PSPACE-complete set (too large to sit comfortably on a tape) can easily be reduced to an NEXP-complete problem, and that the typical element as futurescenario79 has noted, provides a reasonable example of a function.

* Pointers, Produced by rules similar to the standard interpretations of reference, are standard way that recursion, the Halting problem, and NP-complete problems are dealt with, which often has a one-to-one correspondence with a single surveyor token of the pointer, and the benefit of being a recognizable language. These are less vague than one-way Turing mechanisms, which ought to be possible if the same legal definition of a circuit yielded PSPACE. Examples of non-Common Lisp syntax for Turing mechanisms are as follows: *"Step input of two segments - a batch of live tokens of pointer x and their children y, and a set of live tokens of pointer x", "perform computation*, and "return result from pointer y."* [footnote: Further clarification is that the set could be a sequential mix of inputs to various pointers. The distinction to an array solution is that an array is the mix of all sets input to each cell, without a physical division of thunks from nodes, or numbers from adders.]

* In general, a stricter condition must be imposed, instead of the black box of a Map function. This is because an intermediary language used by people in picking problems need not be mathematically useful in the final interpretation; so this Is-a relation is important for P = PSPACE as to avoid object-substitutions creating a solution that PSPACE ≠ NPSPACE.  At the time of scoring: Solving a P vs. NP does not immediately yield the ability to quickly produce human-level expert knowledge, though it may do so side-by-side and once known, even if unrelated. The computational-derived knowledge is very reliant on a Common Lisp variation which standardizes theories and provides a framework: We get one for each theory, such as one for the existence of aliens, one for marginal utility, one for Unicorns, and so on. In this sense, P-BPP is separated from P^BPP, and PSPACE separated from NPSPACE because their interpretative counterparts interfere with each other. From current knowledge, there is no way to provide a specialized Turing mechanism for particularly fast hardware, and resampling from special classes of formulas is still in need to prove P^NP ≠ NP^BPP,-statistical mechanics, selection problems, optimization, combinatorics, number theory, graph theory, game theory, image processing, symbolic integration, linear algebra, and craftserving formula. 

An absence of consensus on the possible interchanging of NP and P, a click-Elster constraint as long as reliable nonce relating is required, and the cumbersome need for splicing proofs represents the reasons a typical Turing mechanism which avoids one-way Turing mechanics requires large amounts of hyper-computation, and where proof is rendered impossible. And the distinction to a halting problem is that the language can prove the impossibility of simulation. The reliability token here is that complex Turing machines don't exist in the formal same manner as today, which is trivialized by PversusNP not resolving, although an Optimum Distribution solution exists.
